title: Tumor Immunotherapy-Related Information on Internet-Based Videos Commonly Used by the Chinese Population: Content Quality Analysis
screen_reason: Although most of the paper is a quality appraisal (PEMAT, DISCERN, JAMA), it also carries a SEPARATE and explicit misinformation coding: two authors independently rated each of 118 videos on a 5-point Likert misinformation scale adapted from Loeb et al., and the paper reports that 12 of the 118 videos contained misinformation. That is a share of items explicitly coded for misinformation against expert judgement, with a stated denominator, so it is a CONTENT prevalence estimate and the paper is not QUALITY-ONLY. The quality instruments are reported alongside but are excluded from prevalence per §3.

estimates.platform: TikTok, Tencent, iQIYI and BiliBili (Chinese video platforms)
estimates.date: Searched 5 March 2022; videos uploaded from 2011 onwards (79% in or after 2018)
estimates.measure_type: % of Chinese-language tumor immunotherapy videos across four video platforms that were coded as containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 12/118 videos (10.2%); 'Only 12 videos contained misinformation (score of >1 out of 5)'; Table 1 'Misinformation score, n (%)': 1 = 6 (5), 2 = 5 (4), 3 = 0 (0), 4 = 1 (1), 5 = 0 (0)
estimates.denominator: 118 videos about tumor immunotherapy retained after screening, drawn from the 50 most-viewed results for the Chinese keyword 'tumor immunotherapy' on each of TikTok, Tencent, iQIYI and BiliBili (200 videos considered; duplicates, paid videos and off-topic videos excluded)
estimates.definition: Video rated above the floor of a 5-point Likert misinformation scale by two independent physician-author coders, i.e. judged to contain some degree of misinformation about tumor immunotherapy
estimates.misinfo_def: No definitional sentence is given; misinformation is operationalised only by instrument - 'We assessed the presence of misinformation using an analogous 5-point Likert scale [16,17]' (the scale is borrowed from Loeb et al's prostate-cancer YouTube study and Herbert et al's pelvic-organ-prolapse study). The framing sentence is 'Dissemination of misinformation through the internet is a major social issue.'
estimates.source_quote: Only 12 videos contained misinformation (score of >1 out of 5).
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); Results, p.3; Table 1, 'Misinformation score, n (%)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors (CN and Y-BF), blinded to each other's ratings and unable to consult one another, independently rated every video; each video's mean of the two ratings was used. An intraclass correlation coefficient was computed to check inter-rater reliability but its value is never reported. The coders are hospital-based clinicians/pharmacists at Shanghai Tenth People's Hospital, so this is expert coding, not fact-checker or crowd adjudication
estimates.moderator_quote: Using the keyword '肿瘤免疫治疗' ('tumor immunotherapy' in Chinese), we searched TikTok, Tencent, iQIYI, and BiliBili on March 5, 2022, which yielded 1820, 395, 400, and 1000 results for each search, respectively. The videos were sorted in accordance with the video's default 'the most viewed' sorting parameter, and the first 50 videos per website were evaluated. [...] We assessed the presence of misinformation using an analogous 5-point Likert scale [16,17]. Videos were independently coded by 2 authors with random coding checks to verify intercoder reliability.
estimates.notes: THRESHOLD INCONSISTENCY an adjudicator must see. The text and abstract both say 'Only 12 videos contained misinformation (score of >1 out of 5)', but Table 1's breakdown sums to 12 only if score=1 videos are counted in (6 + 5 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 12). Under the parenthetical's literal '>1' threshold the count would be 6 videos (5.1%), not 12. I kept 12 because it is the verbatim figure stated twice and it is the one consistent with the table, and 12/118 = 10.2% is an exact part/whole from verbatim counts as R8 allows. The alternative strict reading is 6/118 = 5.1%. Note also that the scale evidently runs 0-5 in practice (the platform means are 0.09-0.4 and 106 videos appear in no score row), so 'score >0' is almost certainly what was meant. Denominator is a most-viewed top-50 slice per platform, hence denom_selection=curated; this is a popularity-weighted sample, not a random or census sample of the platforms' immunotherapy content. Four platforms are pooled in the headline figure; per-platform means exist but only as means, so no per-platform rows are derivable.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen but NOT extracted, with reasons: (1) 'the quality of information was moderate to poor in 54% of videos (overall DISCERN scores of 1-3 out of 5) and 64% of videos (overall JAMA scores of 1-2 out of 4)' - BOTH PERCENTAGES ARE WRONG, and this is worth flagging to an adjudicator as a data-integrity finding. Table 1 gives DISCERN 1 = 2 (2%), 2 = 8 (7%), 3 = 44 (37%), which is 54 VIDEOS, i.e. 45.8% of 118, not 54%; and JAMA 1 = 17 (14%), 2 = 47 (40%), which is 64 VIDEOS, i.e. 54.2%, not 64%. The authors have reported counts as percentages in both cases. I did not create QUALITY rows for these because (a) the stated values are demonstrably incorrect and (b) recovering the correct ones would require a cross-category sum (2+8+44), which R8 forbids. Note also that the DISCERN categories sum to 93 and the JAMA categories to 84, not 118, so 25 and 34 videos respectively must sit at a score of 0 that the table does not display. These are QUALITY measures and excluded from prevalence in any case. (2) PEMAT understandability and actionability - reported as medians (75%, IQR 22-100 and 71%, IQR 0-100; the abstract says 71% and 71%, the table says 75% and 71%, another internal inconsistency). These are median instrument scores, not shares of items, so no row per §3. (3) Per-platform mean misinformation scores (TikTok 0.4 [SD 0.8], Tencent 0.09 [SD 0.3], iQIYI 0.2 [SD 0.8], BiliBili 0.1 [SD 0.4]) and per-publisher-type means (lecture 0.1, interview 0.2, health animation 0.3) - scale MEANS only with no share of videos above a threshold, so excluded per §1 and §2; this is why the paper's claims that 'Videos on Tencent and BiliBili had lesser misinformation than TikTok and iQIYI' and that doctor-led videos contained less misinformation cannot be turned into rows. (4) Table 2 content-completeness distributions (e.g. risk factors: no content 53 (45%), little content 14 (12%)) - completeness scoring is QUALITY, and the paper's summary claim 'more than half of the videos contain little or no content on the risk factors and management' requires a cross-category sum, forbidden by R8. (5) Engagement figures (median forwarding number 12, likes 15, comments 0, subscriptions 0) - no misinformation numerator and no exposure denominator, so no EXPOSURE, REACH or SHARING row is derivable. No CONCENTRATION measure exists. (6) The 3615 videos mentioned in Methods ('the screened 118 of 3615 videos') conflicts with the 1820+395+400+1000 = 3615 raw hits and the 200 videos actually considered; the operative denominator for the misinformation share is unambiguously 118.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content appraisal of Chinese-language online videos. Single Chinese keyword ('tumor immunotherapy') searched on TikTok, Tencent, iQIYI and BiliBili on 5 March 2022, returning 3615 raw hits; the platforms' default 'most viewed' sort was applied and only the top 50 per platform were taken forward (200 videos), from which duplicates, paid videos and off-topic videos were removed, leaving 118. The sample is therefore popularity-weighted and rank-truncated, not representative of platform content, and is limited to one keyword and one language. Misinformation was rated independently by two authors blinded to each other on a 5-point Likert scale adapted from Loeb et al., with the per-video mean used; an intraclass correlation coefficient was said to be computed for inter-rater reliability but no value is reported, which is the study's main reliability weakness. Quality and reliability were separately assessed with PEMAT, a modified 5-item DISCERN and the 4-item JAMA benchmark. Analysis by Mann-Whitney U in GraphPad Prism 8. Ethics approval not required (public data); registered ChiCTR2400081071. The paper carries a published correction, and contains several internal numerical inconsistencies: counts reported as percentages for the DISCERN and JAMA summaries, a misinformation threshold in the text ('>1') that contradicts its own table, and PEMAT understandability given as 71% in the abstract but 75% in Table 1. No response rate applies.
rob.item6_quote: We assessed the presence of misinformation using an analogous 5-point Likert scale [16,17]. Videos were independently coded by 2 authors with random coding checks to verify intercoder reliability. Each video was rated separately, and its mean score was calculated.
rob.item10_quote: Only 12 videos contained misinformation (score of >1 out of 5).
